argument: Let G be a connected double-critical k-chromatic graph. For any vertex v with a neighbour u, chi(G-v) <= chi(G-u-v)+1 = k-1, so G is vertex-critical. A vertex-critical k-chromatic graph that contains K_k equals K_k, so if G is not K_k then it has no k-clique. Apply Erdős–Lovász Tihany with k1=2, k2=k-1: we get disjoint G1 (2-chromatic, so it contains an edge xy) and G2 with chi = k-1 lying inside G-x-y. This contradicts chi(G-x-y)=k-2. So the k1=2 case of the source implies the target, and the target's context says it is a special case of the Erdős–Lovász problem.

The direction is reversed from the seed: Gyárfás–Sumner implies the triangle-free tree statement. If a triangle-free graph G omitted some finite tree T as an induced subgraph, then every finite subgraph of G would be triangle-free and T-free. It would therefore have chromatic number at most f_T(2). By de Bruijn–Erdős compactness, chi(G) <= f_T(2) is finite, a contradiction. The source node's context states this derivation explicitly. The converse (from omega=2 to all omega) is not a known reduction, so the relation is implies, not equivalent_to.

The unit-distance graph is a spanning subgraph of the odd-distance graph, so chi(R^2) <= chi(O). This gives only an inequality between the two unknowns; neither open question settles the other. Determining chi(R^2) (known to lie in 5..7) says nothing about whether chi(O) is infinite, and chi(O) = infinity says nothing about chi(R^2). The target's context explicitly calls the question a relative of the unit-distance colouring problem. So the link is documented but there is no implication.

Goldberg's conjecture is trivially true for simple graphs by Vizing's theorem (chi' <= Delta+1), so its content lies entirely in multigraphs. The 1-factorization conjecture asks the finer question of whether chi' = Delta for dense simple regular graphs. Neither statement implies the other: Goldberg gives nothing beyond Delta+1 for simple graphs, and the 1-factorization conjecture says nothing about multigraphs. The only shared theme is overfull subgraphs in edge-colouring (the relevant link is the Chetwynd–Hilton overfull conjecture, not Goldberg). No documented direct connection appears in either node.

Smith's conjecture is about how two distinct longest cycles intersect. Thomassen's chord conjecture is about a structural property (having a chord) of a single longest cycle in a 3-connected graph. There is no reduction either way: a graph with a unique longest cycle satisfies Smith's statement vacuously, whatever happens with chords, and chords give no information about intersections. The shared topic, longest cycles in highly connected graphs, is too generic for a documented relation, and neither node mentions the other.

Both are Gallai-type questions about the intersection of longest cycles and paths, and they are treated side by side in that literature (e.g. the Shabbir–Zamfirescu–Zamfirescu survey on intersecting longest paths and cycles; not fetched here). Neither implies the other. One is about pairs of longest cycles in k-connected graphs meeting in >= k vertices; the other is about triples of longest paths in connected graphs sharing one vertex. The connection is real as an analogy but was not verified by a citation I fetched, hence plausible.
